sections.title: Sounds, length and stress
sections.summary: Finnish spelling is almost perfectly phonetic, but vowel and consonant length changes meaning and stress always sits on the first syllable. This chapter covers the letters, the double-letter rule and the three front vowels ä, ö and y.

rules.title: One letter, one sound
rules.body: Every letter is pronounced and each letter always stands for the same sound. There are no silent letters, and spelling tells you exactly how to say a word. The vowels a, e, i, o, u are short and pure, roughly as in Spanish or Italian, never reduced to a schwa in unstressed syllables.

rules.title: Double letters are long
rules.body: A doubled vowel or consonant is held about twice as long, and this length is meaningful: tuli (fire), tuuli (wind) and tulli (customs) are three different words. Long consonants are held mid-word, like the k in English 'bookcase'. Always listen for and write length carefully.

rules.title: The front vowels ä, ö and y
rules.body: ä, ö and y are separate letters with their own sounds, not accented a, o and u. ä is like the a in 'cat'; ö is like German ö or the vowel in 'bird' with rounded lips; y is like French u or German ü (say 'ee' with rounded lips). They can also be doubled: pää, yö, työ.

rules.title: Stress is always on the first syllable
rules.body: The main stress falls on the first syllable of every word, including long words and loanwords. Longer words get a lighter secondary stress on the third, fifth and so on syllable, but never on the last. Stress does not lengthen the vowel, so stressed short vowels stay short.

rules.title: Diphthongs
rules.body: Two different vowels in one syllable form a diphthong, pronounced as a smooth glide: ai, ei, oi, ui, yi, äi, öi, au, ou, eu, iu, ie, uo, yö, äy, öy, ey. The pairs ie, uo and yö are especially common. A doubled vowel (aa, ii) is a long single sound, not a diphthong.

rules.title: Consonants
rules.body: Native Finnish words use few consonants: b, c, f, g (except in ng), q, w, x and z appear only in loanwords, and d mostly appears as a result of gradation (katu, kadun). j sounds like English y in 'yes', r is rolled, and h is always pronounced, even before a consonant (kahvi) or at the end of a syllable.

rules.title: nk and ng
rules.body: The pair ng is pronounced as a long [ŋŋ] sound, like the ng in English 'singer' held longer, with no hard g. The pair nk is [ŋk], as in English 'think'. These two alternate under consonant gradation: Helsinki, Helsingissä.

rules.title: Syllables
rules.body: A syllable usually begins with a consonant and contains one vowel, a long vowel or a diphthong: ra-vin-to-la, kau-pun-ki, ta-lo. Two vowels that do not form a diphthong belong to different syllables: pi-an (soon), sa-no-a (to say). Knowing where syllables break helps you hear stress and length.

exercises.explain: tuuli with a long uu is 'wind'; tuli is 'fire', tulli is 'customs' and tulla is 'to come'.

exercises.q: Finnish words are always stressed on the first syllable.
exercises.explain: Main stress is fixed on the first syllable of every word, including loanwords.

exercises.q: Which syllable of 'ravintola' (restaurant) carries the main stress?
exercises.explain: Main stress is always on the first syllable: RA-vin-to-la.

exercises.q: The Finnish word for 'fire' is ___ (one short u, one short l).
exercises.explain: tuli with all short sounds is 'fire'; doubling the u or the l gives a different word.

exercises.q: The letter ä sounds most like the vowel in which English word?
exercises.explain: ä is an open front vowel like the a in 'cat'; 'father' has the sound of Finnish a.

exercises.q: Finnish j is pronounced like the j in English 'jam'.
exercises.explain: Finnish j is like English y in 'yes': joki sounds like 'yoki'.

exercises.q: The Finnish word for 'night' is ___ (y followed by ö).
exercises.explain: yö is a diphthong of the two front vowels y and ö.
kukka with a long kk is 'flower'; kuka with a short k is 'who'.

exercises.q: Doubling a vowel or a consonant can change the meaning of a Finnish word.
exercises.explain: Length is phonemic: mato (worm) and matto (carpet) differ only in the length of the t.

exercises.q: Which word contains a long vowel?
exercises.explain: maa (land) has the long vowel aa; koira has the diphthong oi, and kala and talo have only short vowels.

exercises.q: The Finnish word for 'head' is ___ (p + long ä).
exercises.explain: pää is written with a double ä because the vowel is long.

exercises.q: The ng in 'kengät' is pronounced like the ng in English 'singer', with no hard g sound.
exercises.explain: Finnish ng is a long [ŋŋ] sound; there is never a separate g after it.

exercises.q: Which pair of words differs only in vowel length?
exercises.explain: tuli and tuuli differ in the length of the u; the other pairs differ in consonant length.

pairs: like French u or German ü
like German ö, the vowel in 'bird' with rounded lips

exercises.q: The Finnish verb 'to come' is ___ (tul + double l + a).
exercises.explain: tulla has a long ll; with a short l it would be tuli, 'fire'.
ra-vin-to-la has four syllables, each with one vowel.

exercises.q: In 'tie' (road) the vowels i and e form one syllable, a diphthong.
exercises.explain: ie is one of the common Finnish diphthongs, so tie is a single syllable.
matto with a long tt is 'carpet'; mato is 'worm'.

exercises.q: The Finnish word for 'flower' is ___ (ku + double k + a).
exercises.explain: kukka has a long kk; kuka with a single k means 'who'.

exercises.q: Finnish h is silent before a consonant, as in 'kahvi'.
exercises.explain: h is always pronounced in Finnish, so kahvi is said with an audible h.

exercises.q: Which of these is NOT a Finnish diphthong?
exercises.explain: oa is not a diphthong; in a word like 'sanoa' the o and a belong to separate syllables.

exercises.q: In a long word like 'ravintolassa' a lighter secondary stress falls on the third syllable.
exercises.explain: After the main stress on the first syllable, secondary stress falls on odd syllables (third, fifth), never the last.

sections.title: Vowel harmony and consonant gradation
sections.summary: Two sound rules shape almost every Finnish word: vowel harmony decides whether an ending is spelled with a/o/u or ä/ö/y, and consonant gradation makes k, p and t weaken when a syllable closes. Learn them early and the endings in later chapters will make sense.

rules.title: Back, front and neutral vowels
rules.body: The vowels fall into three groups: back vowels a, o, u; front vowels ä, ö, y; and neutral vowels e, i. A native word contains either back or front vowels, never both. Neutral vowels can appear with either group.

rules.title: Endings follow the word's vowels
rules.body: Every ending that contains a, o or u has a front twin with ä, ö or y. A back-vowel word takes the back version (-ssa, -ko, -a) and a front-vowel word takes the front version (-ssä, -kö, -ä). A word with only e and i counts as a front-vowel word.

examples.en: in the house – in the forest
Are you coming? – Are you eating?

rules.title: Compounds and loanwords
rules.body: In a compound word the last part decides the ending: kirjahylly (bookshelf) gives kirjahyllyssä. Loanwords may mix front and back vowels; then the last non-neutral vowel usually decides, as in olympialaisissa. Usage varies for some loanwords, and dictionaries show both forms.

rules.title: Consonant gradation: kk, pp, tt
rules.body: When an ending closes the last syllable of a word (for example genitive -n or inessive -ssa), a double kk, pp or tt weakens to a single k, p or t. The full form is called the strong grade and the weakened one the weak grade. This happens in nouns, adjectives and verbs.

rules.title: Single k, p, t
rules.body: A single k, p or t also weakens, but in a different way: k usually disappears (joki, joen), p becomes v (lupa, luvan) and t becomes d (katu, kadun). Between two u's or two y's, k becomes v instead of vanishing: puku, puvun; kyky, kyvyn.

rules.title: Clusters with a nasal or liquid
rules.body: When k, p or t follows n, l, r or m, the cluster assimilates: nk becomes ng, mp becomes mm, nt becomes nn, lt becomes ll and rt becomes rr. These are the same weak-grade rule in a different shape. Clusters sk, st, tk and hk do not gradate at all: koski, kosken; matka, matkan.

rules.title: Gradation in verbs
rules.body: Verbs gradate too. In type 1 verbs the infinitive has the strong grade, and the personal endings -n, -t, -mme, -tte close the syllable and trigger the weak grade: lukea gives luen, luet, luemme, luette, but lukee and lukevat keep the strong grade. The negative form also uses the weak stem: en lue, en ota.

examples.en: to read – I read – he/she reads
to take – I take – he/she takes
to give – I give – he/she gives

rules.title: Reverse gradation
rules.body: Some words show the opposite direction: the dictionary form is weak and the inflected forms are strong. This happens with nouns ending in -e (osoite, osoitteen; huone, huoneen) and with type 4 verbs (tavata, tapaan; hakata, hakkaan). Learn these as a pattern rather than as exceptions.

exercises.q: Which group contains only front vowels?
exercises.explain: ä, ö and y are the front vowels; a, o, u are back vowels and e, i are neutral.

exercises.q: e and i are neutral vowels, and a word containing only them takes front-vowel endings.
exercises.explain: Neutral vowels fit either group, but on their own they select the front endings: kielessä.
talo has back vowels, so the ending is -ssa with a back a.
metsä has front vowels, so the ending is -ssä.

exercises.q: What is the genitive ('of the shop') of kauppa?
exercises.explain: The -n closes the syllable, so pp weakens to p: kaupan.

exercises.q: In 'kaupan' the double p becomes a single p because the ending -n closes the syllable.
exercises.explain: A closed syllable triggers the weak grade: pp becomes p.

exercises.en: The book is in the shop.

exercises.explain: A single k usually disappears in the weak grade: joki becomes joen.
A single p weakens to v: lupa becomes luvan.
The cluster nk weakens to ng: kengän.
nt assimilates to nn in the weak grade: rannan.
lt becomes ll in the weak grade, so the genitive is illan.
The t weakens to d and the front-vowel word takes -llä: pöydällä.
tt weakens to t before the closing -n: tytön.

exercises.q: In a compound word the ending follows the vowels of the last part: kirjahylly → kirjahyllyssä.
exercises.explain: Only the final part of a compound decides the vowel harmony of the ending.
tulla has the back vowel u, so the question particle is -ko.
syödä has front vowels, so the particle is -kö: Syötkö?

exercises.q: Which word keeps its k unchanged in the genitive?
exercises.explain: The cluster sk never gradates: koski, kosken.

exercises.q: The genitive of 'puku' (suit) is 'puvun', because k between two u's becomes v.
exercises.explain: Between u-u or y-y a single k becomes v instead of disappearing.

exercises.en: The girl's book is on the table.

exercises.explain: The ending -n closes the syllable and the k disappears: luen.
nt weakens to nn in the first person: annan.
Nouns in -e show reverse gradation: the inflected form has the strong tt.

exercises.q: In 'tavata' (to meet) the first-person form 'tapaan' has the strong grade, the opposite direction from nouns like kauppa.
exercises.explain: Type 4 verbs have a weak infinitive and strong personal forms.
nk becomes ng and the ending is the front form -ssä.
yö has front vowels, so the ending is -ssä.

sections.title: Pronouns, 'to be' and spoken forms
sections.summary: The personal pronouns, the verb olla (to be) and the lack of articles are the backbone of your first sentences. Finnish also has a distinct spoken register with shorter pronouns and verb forms that you will hear from day one.

rules.title: Personal pronouns
rules.body: The pronouns are minä (I), sinä (you, singular), hän (he or she), me (we), te (you, plural or polite) and he (they). Finnish has no grammatical gender, so hän covers both he and she. Note that he means 'they', not 'he'.

rules.title: olla, to be
rules.body: The present tense of olla is olen, olet, on, olemme, olette, ovat. It is irregular only in the third person (on, ovat); the other forms are built on the stem ole-. It also serves in 'I have' sentences (minulla on) and in the perfect tense.

rules.title: Dropping the pronoun
rules.body: Because the verb ending shows the person, minä, sinä, me and te are often left out: Olen opiskelija. Olet oikeassa. The third-person pronouns hän and he are normally kept, because on and ovat do not show who is meant. In speech the pronouns are usually kept for all persons.

rules.title: No articles
rules.body: Finnish has no words for 'a' or 'the'. Talo means 'a house' or 'the house' depending on context, and word order carries some of that meaning: known information comes first and new information last. Do not try to translate the English articles.

examples.en: There is a house over there.

rules.title: Negative forms of olla
rules.body: Negation uses the negative verb ei, which takes the personal endings, followed by the bare stem ole: en ole, et ole, ei ole, emme ole, ette ole, eivät ole. The word 'not' is thus a verb that agrees with the subject.

rules.title: Demonstratives
rules.body: tämä (this), tuo (that) and se (it, that) have the plurals nämä (these), nuo (those) and ne (they, those). se and ne refer to things in standard Finnish, but in speech they replace hän and he for people too.

rules.title: Possession: minun kirjani
rules.body: 'My book' uses the genitive of the pronoun plus a possessive suffix on the noun: minun kirjani, sinun kirjasi, hänen kirjansa, meidän kirjamme, teidän kirjanne, heidän kirjansa. In writing the pronoun can be dropped for the first and second persons (kirjani), but hänen and heidän must stay.

rules.title: Spoken pronouns and olla
rules.body: In everyday speech minä and sinä become mä and sä, hän becomes se and he becomes ne. The verb olla becomes mä oon, sä oot, se on, me ollaan, te ootte, ne on. The possessive suffix is dropped: mun kirja, sun auto. Learn both registers but write the standard forms.

rules.title: Asking who and what
rules.body: Kuka (who) and mikä (what, which) combine with on for the simplest questions: Kuka hän on? Mikä tämä on? The answer repeats the pattern: Hän on Pekka. Tämä on kirja. Kuka and mikä stand at the start of the sentence.

exercises.explain: Finnish has no gendered pronouns, so hän covers both he and she.

exercises.q: Finnish has no words for 'a' and 'the'.
exercises.explain: Definiteness is shown by context and word order, not by articles.
The first person singular of olla is olen.
The first person plural of olla is olemme.
The third person singular of olla is the irregular form on.

exercises.q: What is the usual spoken form of 'minä'?
exercises.explain: minä shortens to mä in speech; sä is 'you' and se replaces hän.

exercises.q: In spoken Finnish 'se' is often used for a person instead of 'hän'.
exercises.explain: Colloquial Finnish uses se and ne for people as well as things.
The second person plural of olla is olette.
The third person plural of olla is ovat.
The ending -n already shows the first person, so the pronoun can be dropped.
The negative verb takes the ending (en) and olla stays in its bare stem ole.
The third person singular of the negative verb is ei.

exercises.q: 'my book' in standard written Finnish is ?
exercises.explain: The genitive minun combines with the possessive suffix -ni on the noun.

exercises.q: The Finnish word 'he' means 'he' (a male person).
exercises.explain: he is the plural pronoun 'they'; 'he or she' is hän.

exercises.q: Which is the spoken form of 'olen'?
exercises.explain: mä oon is the colloquial 'I am'; oot is 'you are' and ollaan is 'we are'.
In speech olet becomes oot.

exercises.q: 'Me ollaan' is the spoken equivalent of 'me olemme'.
exercises.explain: Colloquial Finnish uses the passive form ollaan for 'we are'.
kuka means 'who', so the question asks who the person is.
mikä asks 'what' or 'which' about a thing.
emme is the first person plural of the negative verb, followed by the stem ole.

exercises.q: In spoken Finnish 'ne' is used for ?
exercises.explain: ne replaces he (they) in speech and is also the plural of se.

exercises.q: Ette ___ myöhässä. (you plural are not late)
exercises.explain: After the negative verb, olla appears in its bare stem ole.

sections.title: Verb types and the present tense
sections.summary: Finnish verbs fall into six types that differ in how the stem is found from the infinitive. Once you have the stem, the same personal endings work for every verb, and the negative is built with the conjugated word ei.

rules.title: Type 1: -a/-ä after a vowel
rules.body: Type 1 verbs end in two vowels, the last being a or ä: puhua, sanoa, lukea, kysyä. Remove the final -a/-ä to get the stem (puhu-), then add the personal endings -n, -t, lengthened vowel, -mme, -tte, -vat/-vät: puhun, puhut, puhuu, puhumme, puhutte, puhuvat. Gradation applies: lukea gives luen, luet, lukee.

rules.title: Type 2: -da/-dä
rules.body: Type 2 verbs end in -da/-dä: syödä, juoda, saada, voida, tehdä, nähdä. Remove -da/-dä to get the stem (syö-). The third person singular does not lengthen anything, because the stem already ends in a long vowel or diphthong: hän syö, he syövät. tehdä and nähdä have the stems tee-/tekee and näe-/näkee.

rules.title: Type 3: -la, -na, -ra, -sta
rules.body: Type 3 verbs end in -lla/-llä, -nna/-nnä, -rra/-rrä or -sta/-stä: tulla, mennä, purra, nousta, olla. Remove the last two letters and add -e-: tule-, mene-, nouse-. Then tulen, tulet, tulee, tulemme, tulette, tulevat. Verbs like ajatella show the strong grade here: ajattelen.

rules.title: Type 4: -ata/-ätä, -ota, -uta
rules.body: Type 4 verbs end in a vowel + -ta/-tä: haluta, pelata, tavata, herätä. Remove the -t- so the stem ends in a vowel plus a/ä: halua-, pelaa-, tapaa-. Then haluan, haluat, haluaa, haluamme, haluatte, haluavat. Gradation is reversed: the infinitive is weak and the present is strong (tavata, tapaan).

rules.title: Types 5 and 6
rules.body: Type 5 verbs end in -ita/-itä: tarvita, häiritä, valita. Replace -ta/-tä with -tse-: tarvitsen, tarvitset, tarvitsee, tarvitsemme, tarvitsette, tarvitsevat. Type 6 verbs end in -eta/-etä and mostly mean 'to become': vanheta (grow old), lämmetä (warm up). Replace -ta with -ne-: vanhenen, vanhenee; lämpenee.

rules.title: The personal endings
rules.body: The endings are the same for all types: -n (minä), -t (sinä), lengthened final vowel (hän), -mme (me), -tte (te), -vat/-vät (he). The third person singular doubles the stem's last vowel only when it is a single short vowel: puhuu, tulee, haluaa, tarvitsee; after a long vowel or diphthong nothing is added: syö, saa, voi.

examples.target: puhun, puhut, puhuu, puhumme, puhutte, puhuvat
examples.en: I speak, you speak, he/she speaks, we speak, you speak, they speak

examples.target: syön, syöt, syö, syömme, syötte, syövät
examples.en: I eat, you eat, he/she eats, we eat, you eat, they eat

rules.title: The negative: ei + stem
rules.body: To negate, conjugate the negative verb ei for person (en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät) and follow it with the main verb's stem without any ending. This stem is the second person form minus -t: puhut gives en puhu; syöt gives en syö; tulet gives en tule; haluat gives en halua; tarvitset gives en tarvitse. The weak grade stays: luet, en lue.

rules.title: The present also means the future
rules.body: Finnish has no separate future tense. The present covers both 'I go' and 'I will go'; a time word such as huomenna (tomorrow) or ensi viikolla (next week) makes the future reading clear. Pronouns minä, sinä, me and te are often dropped because the ending shows the person.

examples.en: Tomorrow I will go to work.
I'll call you in the evening.

rules.title: Spoken present forms
rules.body: In speech the first person plural is replaced by the passive form: me mennään, me puhutaan, me syödään (instead of menemme, puhumme, syömme). The third person plural uses the singular verb: ne menee, ne puhuu (instead of he menevät). You will hear these constantly, but standard writing keeps the full forms.

exercises.explain: puhua ends in a vowel + a, so it is a type 1 verb with the stem puhu-.
Stem puhu- plus the first person ending -n.

exercises.q: In type 1 verbs the stem is found by removing the final -a/-ä: puhua → puhu-.
exercises.explain: Type 1 infinitives end in a vowel plus a/ä, and dropping that gives the stem.
Remove -dä to get the stem syö- and add -t.
The stem juo- already ends in a diphthong, so the third person adds nothing.
Verbs in -lla/-llä are type 3; the stem adds -e-: tule-.
Type 3: tul- + e + n = tulen.

exercises.q: 'Hän tulee' is the third person singular of 'tulla'.
exercises.explain: The stem tule- lengthens its final vowel in the third person: tulee.
Type 4: remove -t- to get halua- and add -n.
Type 5: -ita becomes -itse- and the third person lengthens the e: tarvitsee.
The negative verb carries the person (en) and the main verb is the bare stem puhu.
The third person plural of the negative verb is eivät.

exercises.q: The negative verb ei is conjugated for person (en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät) while the main verb stays in its stem form.
exercises.explain: Only the negative word changes; the main verb is the same stem for every person.
The ending -n closes the syllable, so the k disappears: luen.
Type 3: men- + e + mme = menemme.
tehdä has the strong stem teke- in the third person: tekee.
tehdä has the weak stem tee- in the first person: teen.

exercises.q: The first person of 'tavata' (to meet) is 'tavaan'.
exercises.explain: Type 4 verbs have reverse gradation: the present is strong, tapaan.
Verbs ending in -ita/-itä are type 5 and take the stem -itse-.

exercises.q: Huomenna minä ___ töihin. (mennä, I will go)
exercises.explain: The present tense expresses the future; mennä gives menen.

exercises.q: Finnish has no separate future tense; the present tense is used instead.
exercises.explain: Time words like huomenna show that the present refers to the future.

exercises.q: The spoken form of 'we go' (me menemme) is ?
exercises.explain: Spoken Finnish uses the passive form mennään for the first person plural.
Type 4: pelaa- + t = pelaat.

exercises.q: 'Hän ei tarvitse' is the correct negative of 'tarvita'.
exercises.explain: The negative stem is the second person form minus -t: tarvitset gives ei tarvitse.

sections.title: The partitive
sections.summary: The partitive is the most used case after the basic form. It marks indefinite amounts, objects of negative sentences, nouns after numbers, many fixed greetings and the objects of certain verbs. Mastering it unlocks everyday Finnish.

rules.title: Forming the partitive
rules.body: There are three endings. After a single short vowel add -a/-ä: talo, taloa; kirja, kirjaa; kala, kalaa. After a long vowel, a diphthong or a consonant add -ta/-tä: maa, maata; tie, tietä; mies, miestä. Words ending in -e take -tta/-ttä: huone, huonetta; perhe, perhettä. The partitive uses the strong grade (kukka, kukkaa).

rules.title: Old -i words
rules.body: Many old words ending in -i have a stem in -e- and a partitive in -ta/-tä added to a consonant: kieli, kieltä; vesi, vettä; uusi, uutta; pieni, pientä; lapsi, lasta. Newer -i words simply add -a: lasi, lasia; kaupunki, kaupunkia; Suomi, Suomea.

rules.title: After numbers and quantity words
rules.body: After any number except yksi (one), the noun stands in the partitive singular: kaksi kirjaa, kolme taloa, viisi euroa. The same applies after monta (many), paljon (a lot of), vähän (a little) and pari (a couple of): monta ihmistä, paljon rahaa, vähän maitoa.

rules.title: Indefinite amounts
rules.body: A partitive object means 'some of' a substance or an unspecified quantity: Juon kahvia (I drink coffee, some coffee). Compare the total object Juon kahvin (I drink the coffee, the whole cup). Mass nouns and abstract things are therefore usually in the partitive: Haluan vettä. Tarvitsen apua.

rules.title: Negative sentences
rules.body: The object of a negative sentence is always in the partitive, no matter what it would be in the positive: Ostan auton, but En osta autoa. The same holds for 'I have' sentences: Minulla ei ole autoa. Minulla ei ole aikaa.

rules.title: Verbs that always take the partitive
rules.body: Some verbs take a partitive object because they express feelings, ongoing or incomplete actions: rakastaa (love), odottaa (wait for), etsiä (look for), auttaa (help), pelätä (fear), ajatella (think about), harrastaa (do as a hobby). Rakastan sinua. Odotan bussia. An action in progress also uses the partitive: Luen kirjaa (I am reading a book).

rules.title: Pronouns in the partitive
rules.body: The partitive forms of the personal pronouns are minua, sinua, häntä, meitä, teitä, heitä, and the demonstratives are tätä, tuota, sitä. They are the forms you need after negation and after verbs like rakastaa and odottaa: Hän odottaa minua. En tunne häntä.

rules.title: Greetings and wishes
rules.body: Wishes are in the partitive because they imply 'I wish you (some) good ...': Hyvää päivää (good day), Hyvää yötä (good night), Hyvää joulua (merry Christmas), Hyvää ruokahalua (enjoy your meal), Onnea (congratulations, good luck). Kiitos paljon (thanks a lot) belongs to the same pattern.

rules.title: Partitive plural and prepositions
rules.body: The partitive plural ends in -ja/-jä after a short vowel (kirjoja, taloja) or -ia/-iä and -ita/-itä elsewhere (ihmisiä, huoneita). It marks an indefinite number of countable things: Ostan kirjoja (I buy books). Plural predicates also use it: He ovat opiskelijoita. A few prepositions take the partitive too: ilman rahaa (without money), ennen joulua (before Christmas).

exercises.explain: After a single short vowel the partitive ending is -a: taloa.
After a number greater than one the noun is in the partitive singular: kirjaa.

exercises.q: After numbers greater than one the noun is in the partitive singular.
exercises.explain: kaksi kirjaa, kolme taloa: the noun stays singular but takes the partitive ending.
Numbers take the partitive singular: kolme euroa.
An indefinite amount of a substance is in the partitive: kahvia.
In a negative sentence the object is in the partitive: autoa.

exercises.q: In a negative sentence the object is normally in the partitive.
exercises.explain: Negation always triggers the partitive object: En osta autoa.

exercises.q: En näe ___. (hän, I don't see him/her)
exercises.explain: The partitive of hän is häntä, required after negation.

exercises.q: What is the partitive singular of 'vesi' (water)?
exercises.explain: vesi is an old -i word with the consonant-stem partitive vettä.
Wishes are in the partitive; after the diphthong yö the ending is -tä.

exercises.q: 'Rakastan sinut' is the correct way to say 'I love you'.
exercises.explain: rakastaa always takes a partitive object: Rakastan sinua.

exercises.q: Odotan ___ (bussi, I'm waiting for the bus)
exercises.explain: odottaa takes a partitive object: bussia.
The partitive of sinä is sinua.

exercises.q: Which word is NOT in the partitive?
exercises.explain: kirjan ends in -n and is the genitive; the others have partitive endings.
An indefinite amount of water is in the partitive: vettä.

exercises.q: The number 'yksi' (one) takes the partitive: 'yksi kirjaa'.
exercises.explain: yksi takes the basic form: yksi kirja; only numbers from two upwards take the partitive.
Words ending in -e take -tta/-ttä: perhettä.

exercises.q: paljon ___ (ihminen, a lot of people; partitive plural)
exercises.explain: paljon takes the partitive, and for countable people the plural ihmisiä is used.
An indefinite number of countable things takes the partitive plural kirjoja.

exercises.q: 'Luen kirjaa' means I am reading a book, an ongoing and unfinished action.
exercises.explain: The partitive object marks an action in progress; Luin kirjan would mean I read the whole book.
The preposition ilman takes the partitive: ilman rahaa.

exercises.en: He/she is waiting for the bus at the station.

pairs: genitive: the whole coffee as a total object

exercises.q: What is the partitive singular of 'kieli' (language)?
exercises.explain: kieli is an old -i word: its partitive singular is kieltä (kieliä is the plural).

sections.title: The six local cases and the genitive
sections.summary: Where English uses prepositions like in, from, to, on and off, Finnish adds endings to the noun. Three inner cases cover being inside something, three outer cases cover surfaces and places, and the genitive -n marks possession and is used with postpositions.

rules.title: The genitive -n
rules.body: The genitive adds -n to the weak stem: talon, kirjan, kaupan, tytön. It marks the possessor and comes before the thing possessed, exactly like English 's: Pekan auto (Pekka's car), talon ovi (the door of the house). It is also the form used before postpositions and as the total object (chapter 7).

rules.title: Inessive -ssa/-ssä: in
rules.body: The inessive means 'in, inside': talossa (in the house), kaupassa (in the shop), Suomessa (in Finland), Helsingissä (in Helsinki). It attaches to the weak stem. It also covers 'at' for enclosed places like school, work or a café: koulussa, kahvilassa.

examples.en: The book is in the bag.

rules.title: Elative -sta/-stä: out of, from
rules.body: The elative means 'out of, from inside': talosta (from the house), Suomesta (from Finland), Helsingistä (from Helsinki). It also means 'about' with verbs of speaking and thinking: Puhumme Suomesta (we talk about Finland), and it answers Mistä? (from where). It uses the weak stem.

rules.title: Illative: into
rules.body: The illative means 'into, to' and answers Mihin? / Minne? It is formed by lengthening the final vowel and adding -n: taloon, kauppaan, Helsinkiin, Suomeen. After a one-syllable word with a long vowel or diphthong it is -hVn with the same vowel repeated: maahan, työhön, tiehen. Words ending in -e take -seen: huoneeseen. The illative keeps the strong grade: kauppaan, not kaupaan.

rules.title: Adessive -lla/-llä: on, at, by
rules.body: The adessive means 'on top of' or 'at' an open place: pöydällä (on the table), torilla (at the market square), asemalla (at the station), kadulla (on the street). It also expresses the instrument or means: bussilla (by bus), autolla (by car), kynällä (with a pen). It uses the weak stem.

examples.en: The book is on the table.
I go to work by bus.

rules.title: Ablative -lta/-ltä: off, from
rules.body: The ablative means 'from on top of, from at': pöydältä (off the table), torilta (from the market square), asemalta (from the station). With people it means 'from someone': Sain kirjeen Annalta (I got a letter from Anna). It uses the weak stem.

examples.en: I take the book from the table.
I'm coming from the market square.
I got a gift from a friend.

rules.title: Allative -lle: onto, to
rules.body: The allative means 'onto, to the surface of' or 'to a place': pöydälle (onto the table), torille (to the market square), asemalle (to the station). With people it means 'to someone' and marks the receiver: Annan kirjan Pekalle (I give the book to Pekka). It uses the weak stem; there is no vowel-harmony variant.

examples.en: I put the book on the table.
I give the book to Pekka.

rules.title: Inner or outer?
rules.body: Countries and most towns take the inner cases: Suomessa, Helsingissä, Turussa. Some towns take the outer cases by tradition, especially those ending in -lahti, -joki, -mäki and a few others: Tampereella, Rovaniemellä, Seinäjoella, and the country Venäjällä (in Russia). Enclosed places are inner (koulussa, kaupassa); open places and events are outer (torilla, asemalla, kurssilla, pihalla).

rules.title: Postpositions with the genitive
rules.body: Most Finnish 'prepositions' are postpositions that follow a noun in the genitive: talon takana (behind the house), pöydän alla (under the table), kaupan vieressä (next to the shop), koulun edessä (in front of the school), puun päällä (on top of the tree). With pronouns the same forms are used: minun kanssani (with me), sinun kanssasi.

examples.en: The cat is under the table.
The car is behind the house.

exercises.explain: -ssa is the inessive, meaning 'in'.
Suomi has the stem Suome- and takes the inessive -ssa: Suomessa.
The inessive is the 'in' case: talossa, koulussa.
-stä is the elative, 'out of, from', on the weak stem Helsingi-.
The illative lengthens the final vowel and adds -n, keeping the strong grade: kauppaan.
The genitive Pekan before the noun marks possession.
The genitive adds -n to the weak stem: tytön.

exercises.q: The illative (into) keeps the strong grade: kauppa → kauppaan.
exercises.explain: The illative ending does not close the syllable, so the strong pp stays.

exercises.q: 'I go by bus' uses which form of bussi?
exercises.explain: The adessive -lla expresses the means of transport.
The adessive -llä is added to the weak stem pöydä-.

exercises.en: The cat sleeps under the table.

exercises.explain: Tampere takes the outer cases by tradition: Tampereella.
After a long vowel in a one-syllable word the illative is -hVn: maahan.
The receiver takes the allative -lle on the weak stem Peka-.
An open place takes the outer cases, and 'from' is the ablative -lta.
Words ending in -e take the illative -seen on the long stem: huoneeseen.

exercises.q: 'Puhun Suomesta' can mean 'I'm talking about Finland'.
exercises.explain: The elative also expresses the topic after verbs of speaking.
A station is an open place and takes the adessive -lla.
Venäjä is one of the few countries that take the outer case: Venäjällä.
vieressä is a postposition meaning 'next to', and the noun before it is in the genitive.

exercises.q: Auto on ___ takana. (talo, behind the house)
exercises.explain: Postpositions like takana follow a noun in the genitive: talon takana.
After the diphthong yö the illative is -hön, repeating the last vowel.
The illative keeps the strong grade nk and lengthens the i: Helsinkiin.

sections.title: Object cases and 'to have'
sections.summary: The object of a Finnish verb can be in the nominative, the genitive or the partitive, and the choice tells whether the action is complete and whether the object is whole. The same case system builds 'to have' sentences, since Finnish has no verb for having.

rules.title: Three object forms
rules.body: An object can take the genitive -n (kirjan), the partitive (kirjaa) or the nominative (kirja). The genitive and nominative forms are together called the total object, often labelled accusative. The partitive is the partial object. Picking the right one is the heart of Finnish sentence grammar.

rules.title: Total object: the genitive -n
rules.body: Use the genitive object when the action is complete or will be completed and the object is a whole, countable thing: Ostan auton (I'll buy a car), Luin kirjan (I read the book through), Söin omenan (I ate the apple). The sentence must be positive.

rules.title: Partial object: the partitive
rules.body: Use the partitive object when the action is ongoing or incomplete (Luen kirjaa), when the amount is indefinite or a substance (Juon maitoa), when the verb is one that always takes the partitive (Rakastan sinua), and always in a negative sentence (En osta autoa). The partitive is therefore the safe default when in doubt.

examples.en: I was eating an apple / ate some apple.

rules.title: Nominative total object
rules.body: The total object appears in the nominative, without -n, after an imperative (Lue kirja! Osta auto!), in the passive (Kirja luetaan, the book is read) and in necessity constructions with täytyy or pitää (Minun täytyy ostaa auto). A plural total object is also simply the nominative plural: Ostin kirjat (I bought the books).

examples.en: I have to buy a car.

rules.title: Pronoun objects: minut and minua
rules.body: Personal pronouns have a special total-object form ending in -t: minut, sinut, hänet, meidät, teidät, heidät. Their partitive forms are minua, sinua, häntä, meitä, teitä, heitä. Näin hänet (I saw him, completed), but En nähnyt häntä (negative) and Rakastan häntä (partitive verb). Kuka also has the form kenet.

examples.en: I'll invite you to the party.

rules.title: 'To have': minulla on
rules.body: Finnish has no verb 'to have'. The possessor takes the adessive -lla/-llä and olla stands in the third person singular: Minulla on auto (I have a car, literally 'on me is a car'). The pronoun forms are minulla, sinulla, hänellä, meillä, teillä, heillä; with nouns: Pekalla on kissa. In speech: mulla, sulla, sillä, niillä.

rules.title: Negative 'have'
rules.body: The negative is minulla ei ole, and the thing possessed goes into the partitive, as in every negative sentence: Minulla ei ole autoa. Meillä ei ole aikaa. Hänellä ei ole rahaa. The verb stays ei ole regardless of how many things are missing.

rules.title: What case after 'on'?
rules.body: After minulla on, a whole countable thing stands in the nominative (Minulla on auto, Minulla on kaksi lasta with the number rule), while a substance or an indefinite amount is in the partitive (Minulla on rahaa, Minulla on aikaa). The question is Onko sinulla ...? and the short answers are On and Ei ole.

examples.en: Yes, I do. / No, I don't.

rules.title: Feelings with minulla on
rules.body: Many states that English expresses with 'I am' use the have-construction: Minulla on nälkä (I'm hungry), Minulla on jano (I'm thirsty), Minulla on kylmä (I'm cold), Minulla on kuuma (I'm hot), Minulla on kiire (I'm in a hurry), Minulla on tylsää (I'm bored). Literally they say 'on me is hunger'.

exercises.explain: Possession uses the adessive possessor plus on: Minulla on auto.

exercises.q: ___ on koira. (sinä, you have a dog)
exercises.explain: The possessor takes the adessive: sinulla.

exercises.q: Finnish has no verb 'to have'; it uses 'olla' with the possessor in the adessive.
exercises.explain: Minulla on literally means 'on me is'.

exercises.q: Luin ___ (kirja, I read the whole book)
exercises.explain: A completed action on a whole object takes the genitive total object: kirjan.

exercises.q: Luen ___. (kirja, I'm reading a book, still going on)
exercises.explain: An ongoing, unfinished action takes the partitive object: kirjaa.
After negation the thing possessed is in the partitive: aikaa.

exercises.q: In a negative sentence the object is always in the partitive.
exercises.explain: Negation rules out the total object: En osta autoa, not En osta auton.

exercises.q: Ostan ___. (auto, I'll buy the car, the whole thing)
exercises.explain: A complete action on a whole object takes the genitive -n: auton.
The total-object form of hän is hänet; the action is complete and the sentence positive.
rakastaa always takes the partitive: häntä.

exercises.q: In 'Lue kirja!' (Read the book!) the object is in the nominative because the verb is an imperative.
exercises.explain: After an imperative the total object has no -n: Lue kirja!
In a necessity construction with täytyy the total object is in the nominative.

exercises.q: En tunne ___. (sinä, I don't know you)
exercises.explain: A negative sentence takes the partitive pronoun sinua.
Noun + -lla + on is the possession pattern: Pekka has a cat.

exercises.q: Meillä ___ ole rahaa. (we don't have money)
exercises.explain: In the have-construction the verb is always third person: ei ole.

exercises.q: 'Minulla on nälkä', literally 'on me is hunger', means 'I am hungry'.
exercises.explain: Finnish expresses many bodily states with the have-construction.
A substance in an indefinite amount is a partitive object: maitoa.

exercises.q: Ostin ___. (kirja, I bought the books, plural total object)
exercises.explain: A plural total object is the nominative plural: kirjat.
mulla is the colloquial form of minulla.

exercises.q: Söin ___. (omena, I ate the apple, the whole of it)
exercises.explain: The whole apple eaten up is a total object in the genitive: omenan.

exercises.en: I ate an apple in the morning.

exercises.q: 'Söin omenaa' means I ate some of the apple or was eating an apple.
exercises.explain: The partitive object leaves the action incomplete or the amount indefinite.
A complete positive action on a pronoun takes the -t form: sinut.

sections.title: Past tense and perfect
sections.summary: The simple past (imperfect) is marked by -i- inserted before the personal ending, with a few predictable vowel changes. The negative past and the perfect both use the past participle in -nut/-nyt, so learning one form gives you three tenses.

rules.title: The past marker -i-
rules.body: The imperfect adds -i- between the stem and the personal ending: puhua gives puhuin, puhuit, puhui, puhuimme, puhuitte, puhuivat. The third person singular is just stem + i with no lengthening. Stems ending in o, u, y or ö keep their vowel: sanoin, puhuin, kysyin.

rules.title: Vowel changes before -i-
rules.body: A stem-final e, i or ä drops before the -i-: tulla, tulin; lukea, luin; etsiä, etsin; pitää, pidin. A stem-final a drops in stems of three or more syllables (rakastaa, rakastin; muistaa, muistin) and in two-syllable stems whose first vowel is o or u (ottaa, otin; sanoa, sanoin keeps the o). In two-syllable stems whose first vowel is a, e or i, the a becomes o: antaa, annoin; maksaa, maksoin; ajaa, ajoin.

rules.title: Long vowels, diphthongs and ti → si
rules.body: A long vowel shortens before -i-: saada, sain; jäädä, jäin. In diphthongs the first vowel stays and the second drops: syödä, söin; juoda, join; viedä, vein; tehdä, tein; nähdä, näin. Type 4 verbs add -si-: haluta, halusin; tavata, tapasin. In some verbs t + i becomes si: tietää, tiesin; löytää, löysin; lentää, lensin. olla gives olin, olit, oli, olimme, olitte, olivat.

rules.title: The past participle -nut/-nyt
rules.body: The past participle is built on the infinitive stem: puhua gives puhunut, syödä gives syönyt, haluta gives halunnut, tarvita gives tarvinnut. For type 3 verbs the final consonant of the infinitive is doubled instead of n: tulla, tullut; mennä, mennyt; nousta, noussut; pestä, pessyt. The plural participle ends in -neet (tulleet, syöneet). olla gives ollut, olleet.

rules.title: Negative past: ei + participle
rules.body: The negative past uses the conjugated negative verb plus the past participle: en puhunut, et puhunut, ei puhunut, emme puhuneet, ette puhuneet, eivät puhuneet. Note that the plural persons take -neet. The object of a negative sentence is in the partitive as usual: En nähnyt häntä.

rules.title: The perfect: olen tehnyt
rules.body: The perfect combines the present of olla with the past participle: olen puhunut, olet puhunut, on puhunut, olemme puhuneet, olette puhuneet, ovat puhuneet. Use it when the result matters now, when the time is unspecified ('have you ever'), or when something that began in the past is still going on: Olen asunut täällä kaksi vuotta (I have lived here for two years).

examples.en: I have lived here for two years.

rules.title: Negative perfect and pluperfect
rules.body: The negative perfect is en ole puhunut, emme ole puhuneet: the negative verb, the stem ole, and the participle. The pluperfect ('had done') uses the past of olla: olin puhunut, olimme puhuneet; negative en ollut puhunut. It describes the earlier of two past events: Olin jo syönyt, kun hän tuli (I had already eaten when he came).

examples.target: Olin jo syönyt, kun hän tuli.
examples.en: I had already eaten when he/she came.

rules.title: Past forms of olla and 'had'
rules.body: olla in the past: olin, olit, oli, olimme, olitte, olivat; negative en ollut, ei ollut, emme olleet; perfect olen ollut. The have-construction follows: Minulla oli auto (I had a car), Minulla ei ollut aikaa (I didn't have time), Minulla on ollut kiire (I have been busy).

rules.title: Time words for the past
rules.body: Common companions of the past tenses: eilen (yesterday), toissapäivänä (the day before yesterday), viime viikolla (last week), viime vuonna (last year), kaksi vuotta sitten (two years ago), äsken (just now), jo (already), vielä (yet, in negative sentences: en vielä, not yet), koskaan (ever, with negation: never).

examples.en: I moved to Finland two years ago.

exercises.explain: The past marker -i- goes before the first person ending: puhu + i + n.
The past of olla in the first person is olin.

exercises.q: The past tense marker in Finnish is -i-.
exercises.explain: The imperfect inserts -i- between the stem and the personal ending.
The stem sano- keeps its o and adds -i: sanoi.
In the diphthong uo the second vowel drops before -i: juo- becomes joi.
In a two-syllable stem with a in the first syllable, a becomes o before -i, and nt weakens to nn: annoin.
The stem-final e drops before -i and the k disappears in the weak grade: luimme.

exercises.q: The first person past of 'ottaa' (to take) is 'otin'.
exercises.explain: With o in the first syllable the stem-final a drops: ott- + i + n, weak grade otin.
The negative past is the conjugated ei plus the participle -nut: en puhunut.
Plural persons take the participle -neet; tulla doubles the l: tulleet.

exercises.q: In the negative past the main verb takes the participle -nut/-nyt in the singular and -neet in the plural.
exercises.explain: en puhunut but emme puhuneet.
The perfect is the present of olla plus the past participle: olen asunut.

exercises.q: Oletko ___ Suomessa? (käydä, Have you been to Finland?)
exercises.explain: The participle of käydä is käynyt, with front vowels -nyt.
Type 3 verbs double the infinitive consonant and use front-vowel -nyt: mennyt.

exercises.q: Olemme ___ täällä kaksi vuotta. (asua, we have lived)
exercises.explain: The plural participle is -neet: olemme asuneet.

exercises.en: I have lived in Finland for three years.

exercises.q: The first person past of 'tietää' (to know) is 'tietin'.
exercises.explain: In tietää the t + i becomes si: tiesin.
Type 4 verbs form the past with -si-: halusin.
The have-construction uses the third person past of olla: oli.
emme ole + participle is the negative perfect.
The participle of olla is ollut, used after ei in the negative past.

exercises.q: 'Maksoin' (I paid) shows the change of a to o before the past marker -i-.
exercises.explain: maksaa has a in its first syllable, so the stem-final a becomes o: maksoin.
Type 3 verbs in -sta double the s in the participle: noussut.
With oi in the first syllable the a drops, and tt weakens to t: soitin.

exercises.q: 'Olin jo syönyt, kun hän tuli' uses the pluperfect for the earlier of two past events.
exercises.explain: olin syönyt (I had eaten) happened before hän tuli (he came).

sections.title: Adjectives, comparison and adverbs
sections.summary: Adjectives take the same case and number as their noun, so one noun phrase can carry the ending twice. Comparison uses the suffixes -mpi and -in, and most adverbs are formed with -sti, with a few irregular forms you will use every day.

rules.title: Adjectives agree with the noun
rules.body: An adjective before a noun takes the same number and case as the noun: iso talo, isossa talossa, isot talot, isoja taloja, isoon taloon. The adjective gradates and changes its stem like a noun: punainen auto, punaisessa autossa; kaunis kaupunki, kauniissa kaupungissa.

examples.en: I live in a big house.

rules.title: Adjectives after 'to be'
rules.body: As a predicate the adjective agrees in number: Talo on iso. With a plural countable subject it goes into the partitive plural: Talot ovat isoja. Lapset ovat pieniä. With a mass noun subject the partitive singular is used: Kahvi on kuumaa. Vesi on kylmää.

rules.title: Comparative -mpi
rules.body: The comparative adds -mpi to the inflectional stem: iso, isompi; pieni, pienempi; kaunis, kauniimpi; uusi, uudempi. In two-syllable adjectives ending in -a/-ä the vowel becomes e: vanha, vanhempi; kova, kovempi; paha, pahempi. 'Than' is kuin: Hän on vanhempi kuin minä. The comparative declines like a noun with the stem -mma-/-mpa-: isomman, isompaa, isommassa.

rules.title: Superlative -in
rules.body: The superlative adds -in to the stem, dropping a final a, ä, e or i: iso, isoin; vanha, vanhin; pieni, pienin; uusi, uusin; kaunis, kaunein. A long vowel shortens: vapaa, vapain. It declines with the stem -imma-/-impa-: isoimman, isointa, isoimmassa. It is often preceded by a genitive: maailman paras (the best in the world).

examples.en: This is the oldest house in the city.
He/she is the smallest in the class.
It is the most beautiful place in the world.

rules.title: Irregular comparison
rules.body: A few very common adjectives are irregular: hyvä, parempi, paras (good, better, best); pitkä, pidempi, pisin (long/tall); and the quantity words paljon, enemmän, eniten (much, more, most) and vähän, vähemmän, vähiten (little, less, least). Learn them as sets.

rules.title: Adverbs in -sti
rules.body: Most adverbs of manner add -sti to the adjective's inflectional stem: nopea, nopeasti (quickly); hidas, hitaasti (slowly); kaunis, kauniisti (beautifully); huono, huonosti (badly); helppo, helposti (easily). The adverb from hyvä is the irregular hyvin (well), and hyvin also means 'very' before an adjective.

rules.title: Comparing adverbs
rules.body: The comparative adverb ends in -mmin and the superlative in -immin: nopeasti, nopeammin, nopeimmin; hitaasti, hitaammin, hitaimmin. Irregular: hyvin, paremmin, parhaiten (well, better, best); paljon, enemmän, eniten; vähän, vähemmän, vähiten. 'Than' is again kuin.

examples.en: You speak Finnish better than before.

rules.title: Intensifiers and 'as ... as'
rules.body: Strengthen an adjective with hyvin, todella, tosi (spoken) or oikein: todella iso (really big), tosi hyvä (really good). 'Too' is liian: liian kallis (too expensive). 'As ... as' is yhtä ... kuin: Hän on yhtä pitkä kuin minä. 'Much bigger' is paljon isompi, and 'a little bigger' is vähän isompi.

examples.target: Hän on yhtä pitkä kuin minä.
examples.en: He/she is as tall as me.

rules.title: Stem changes in common adjectives
rules.body: Adjectives in -nen have the stem -se-: punainen, punaisen, punaista; suomalainen, suomalaisen. Adjectives in -s have a stem with a long vowel: kaunis, kauniin, kaunista; kallis, kalliin, kallista. Those in -in or -ton change too: lämmin, lämpimän, lämmintä; työtön, työttömän. Gradation applies: pitkä, pitkän; helppo, helpon.

exercises.explain: The adjective takes the same case as the noun: isossa talossa.

exercises.q: Talo on ___. (iso, The house is big)
exercises.explain: With a singular subject the predicate adjective is in the basic form: iso.

exercises.q: Finnish adjectives agree with their noun in number and case.
exercises.explain: iso talo, isot talot, isossa talossa: the ending appears on both words.
The comparative suffix -mpi attaches to the stem iso-: isompi.
In a two-syllable adjective ending in -a the a becomes e before -mpi: vanhempi.
The superlative suffix is -in: isoin.
hyvä is irregular: hyvä, parempi, paras.
The superlative is paras; hyvin is the adverb 'well'.
Adverbs of manner add -sti to the stem: nopeasti.
The adverb of hyvä is the irregular hyvin.

exercises.q: Adverbs of manner are usually formed with -sti: kaunis → kauniisti.
exercises.explain: -sti attaches to the inflectional stem kaunii-.

exercises.q: 'punainen auto' in the inessive ('in the red car') is ?
exercises.explain: Adjectives in -nen use the stem -se- and take the same case as the noun.
After a number both adjective and noun are in the partitive singular: isoa taloa.
The final i drops before -in: pienin.

exercises.q: Talot ovat ___. (iso, The houses are big)
exercises.explain: A predicate adjective with a plural countable subject is in the partitive plural: isoja.

exercises.en: This is the best restaurant in the city.

exercises.explain: pitkä is irregular: pidempi, superlative pisin.
The comparative adverb ends in -mmin: nopeammin; nopeimmin is 'most quickly'.
The comparative of the adverb nopeasti is nopeammin.
The superlative adverb of hyvin is parhaiten.

exercises.q: Tarvitsen ___ laukun. (isompi, a bigger bag; genitive object)
exercises.explain: The comparative declines with the stem -mma-: isomman.

exercises.q: 'Hän on yhtä pitkä kuin minä' means 'He/she is as tall as me'.
exercises.explain: yhtä ... kuin is the 'as ... as' construction.
uusi has the stem uude-, so the comparative is uudempi.
The stem kaunii- shortens its vowel before -in: kaunein.

sections.title: Questions, negation and word order
sections.summary: Yes/no questions are made with the particle -ko/-kö, and question words start the sentence. Negation is a verb of its own that pulls in partitive objects and negative pronouns. This chapter also covers numbers and clock time, which you need for everyday questions.

rules.title: Yes/no questions with -ko/-kö
rules.body: Attach -ko (back vowels) or -kö (front vowels) to the word you are asking about and move that word to the front. Usually that is the verb: Puhutko suomea? Onko hän kotona? Oletko väsynyt? Tuletteko mukaan? In speech the particle is shortened to -ks: Puhutsä suomea? Onks se kotona?

rules.title: Answering yes and no
rules.body: The natural answer repeats the verb: Puhutko suomea? Puhun. / En puhu. Onko hän kotona? On. / Ei ole. Kyllä (yes) and joo (yeah, spoken) are also used, often together with the verb: Kyllä puhun. Ei alone works as 'no'.

examples.en: Do you have time? – No (I don't).

rules.title: Question words
rules.body: Question words start the sentence: mikä (what, which), mitä (what, partitive object), kuka (who), kenen (whose), missä (where), mistä (from where), mihin or minne (where to), milloin or koska (when), miksi (why), miten or kuinka (how), kuinka paljon (how much), kuinka monta + partitive (how many), millainen (what kind of).

examples.en: How many children do you have?

rules.title: Word order and emphasis
rules.body: Basic order is subject, verb, object, but word order is flexible: known information comes first and new information last. Pöydällä on kissa (there is a cat on the table) and Kissa on pöydällä (the cat is on the table) both work. The particle -ko can attach to any word to question it: Suomeako hän puhuu? (Is it Finnish that he speaks?).

examples.en: The cat is on the table.
There is a cat on the table.
Is it Finnish that he/she speaks?

rules.title: Negation and negative words
rules.body: ei conjugates (en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät) and the object becomes partitive. Negative questions add -ko to the negative verb: Etkö tule? Eikö hän ole kotona? Negative pronouns and adverbs need ei in the sentence: ei mitään (nothing), ei kukaan (nobody), ei koskaan (never), ei missään (nowhere), ei vielä (not yet), ei enää (no longer).

examples.en: I don't drink coffee any more.

rules.title: vai or tai?
rules.body: Both mean 'or', but vai is used only in questions that offer alternatives and expect one of them as the answer: Kahvia vai teetä? Tuletko vai et? Elsewhere, including questions where either or both can be true, use tai: Haluatko kahvia tai teetä? (would you like coffee or tea, or neither).

examples.en: You can call or send a message.

rules.title: Numbers
rules.body: 1-10: yksi, kaksi, kolme, neljä, viisi, kuusi, seitsemän, kahdeksan, yhdeksän, kymmenen. 11-19 add -toista: yksitoista, kaksitoista. Tens use -kymmentä: kaksikymmentä (20), kolmekymmentä (30); 21 is kaksikymmentäyksi. 100 is sata, 200 kaksisataa, 1000 tuhat. The counted noun is in the partitive singular: kaksikymmentä euroa.

rules.title: Telling the time
rules.body: Ask Mitä kello on? or Paljonko kello on? Answer Kello on kaksi (it is two). Half hours count towards the next hour: puoli kolme is 2:30. Minutes past: viisitoista yli kaksi (2:15, also varttia yli kaksi). Minutes to: viittä vaille kolme (2:55). 'At' a time uses the ablative: kello kahdelta (at two), puoli kolmelta (at half past two). Days take -na: maanantaina (on Monday).

rules.title: Polite requests and common patterns
rules.body: Soften a request with the conditional: Saisinko kahvia? (Could I have a coffee?), Voisitko auttaa? (Could you help?). Anteeksi starts a question to a stranger: Anteeksi, missä on asema? 'Please' has no direct equivalent; ole hyvä means 'here you are' or 'you're welcome', and kiitos covers 'please' in requests: Kahvi, kiitos.

examples.en: Excuse me, where is the station?

exercises.explain: The particle -ko attaches to the conjugated verb puhut, and puhua has back vowels.

exercises.q: ___ hän kotona? (olla, Is he/she at home?)
exercises.explain: on + -ko gives Onko, which moves to the front of the question.

exercises.q: The question particle -ko/-kö attaches to the word being asked about, which moves to the front of the sentence.
exercises.explain: Usually that word is the verb: Tuletko? but it can be another word: Huomennako tulet?
missä asks about location; mistä is 'from where' and minne is 'where to'.
The object of tehdä is asked with the partitive form mitä.

exercises.q: A natural short 'yes' answer to 'Syötkö lihaa?' is ?
exercises.explain: Finnish answers by repeating the verb in the right person: Syön.

exercises.q: To answer 'Tuletko?' with 'yes', you can simply say 'Tulen.'
exercises.explain: Repeating the verb is the standard way of saying yes.
mistä is the elative question word, 'from where'.
The standard form is seitsemän; seittemän is heard in speech but not written.
Tens are formed with -kymmentä: kaksikymmentä.
Finnish counts half hours towards the next hour, so puoli kolme is 2:30.
kukaan needs the negative verb, and ei comes before the participle tullut.
The negative pronoun mitään (anything, nothing) goes with ei.

exercises.q: Kahvia ___ teetä? (coffee or tea, which one do you want?)
exercises.explain: A question offering alternatives uses vai; tai is 'or' elsewhere.
After the negative verb the main verb is the bare stem tule.

exercises.q: 'Pöydällä on kissa' and 'Kissa on pöydällä' are both correct, and the word at the end carries the new information.
exercises.explain: Finnish word order is flexible and follows the known-first, new-last principle.

options: Is it Finnish that he/she speaks?
exercises.explain: The particle -ko on Suomea puts the focus of the question on the language.

exercises.q: Kuinka ___ tämä maksaa? (How much does this cost?)
exercises.explain: kuinka paljon means 'how much'.
The teens add -toista to the unit: yksitoista is eleven.
Days of the week take the essive ending -na: maanantaina.

exercises.en: How many children do you have?

exercises.explain: The time at which something happens takes the ablative -lta: kahdelta.
miksi is 'why'; miten is 'how' and milloin is 'when'.

exercises.q: Spoken 'Onks sulla rahaa?' corresponds to standard '___ sinulla rahaa?'
exercises.explain: The spoken -ks is the standard particle -ko: Onko.

exercises.q: 'Minä en koskaan juo kahvia' means 'I never drink coffee'.
exercises.explain: koskaan with the negative verb means 'never'.
